important_notes: The scandal occurred in 2009 and resulted in Ramalinga Raju's conviction and sentencing.

The scandal has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp. scandal in terms of its scale and impact.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.
evidence.text:

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:

He had founded Satyam in 1987.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.
evidence.text:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

evidence.chunk_content:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

A heavyweight of the nation's software industry, Raju, 60, has been in jail for the past 32 months.

He had founded Satyam in 1987.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

evidence.chunk_content:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.
evidence.text:

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.
evidence.text:

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

evidence.chunk_content:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.
evidence.text:

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

A heavyweight of the nation's software industry, Raju, 60, has been in jail for the past 32 months.

He had founded Satyam in 1987.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

A heavyweight of the nation's software industry, Raju, 60, has been in jail for the past 32 months.

He had founded Satyam in 1987.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.
evidence.text:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

A heavyweight of the nation's software industry, Raju, 60, has been in jail for the past 32 months.

He had founded Satyam in 1987.

His company made giant strides as the outsourcing business grew in India in the 1990s.

evidence.chunk_content:
An Indian software pioneer and nine others have been sentenced to seven years in jail for their role in what has been dubbed India's biggest corporate scandal in memory, police said.

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.
evidence.text:

Ramalinga Raju, the former chairman of software services exporter Satyam Computers Services, was also fined $804,000, R.K.

Gaur, a spokesman for India's Central Bureau of Investigation, told CNN.

evidence.chunk_content:
In 2009, Satyam Computers Services was at the center of a massive $1.6 billion fraud case after its then-chairman Raju admitted inflating profits with fictitious assets and nonexistent cash.

Investigators say losses to investors resulting from the company's book manipulation were much higher.

A special court convicted Raju and nine other people of cheating, criminal conspiracy, breach of public trust and other charges, said the Central Bureau of Investigation, which looked into the case.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the media, the case has been compared to the 2001 Enron Corp.

scandal, in which a Houston energy company's earnings had been overstated by several hundred million dollars.

When the scam made headlines, Satyam, which means "truth" in Sanskrit, was India's fourth-largest software services provider.

It was serving almost 700 companies, including 185 Fortune 500 companies, and generated more than half of its revenue from the United States.

The company had about 53,000 employees and operated in 65 countries.

evidence.chunk_content:
After Raju's shock disclosures six years ago, the Indian government fired Satyam's board.

In a subsequent state-backed auction, the company was bought by Tech Mahindra, part of the country's Mahindra Group.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.
evidence.text:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

evidence.chunk_content:
This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

Fox's "Glee" covered several of the show's most popular songs for a Season 2 episode and even released a special "The Rocky Horror Glee Show" EP.

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

evidence.chunk_content:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.
evidence.text:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

evidence.chunk_content:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.
evidence.text:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

evidence.chunk_content:
This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

Fox's "Glee" covered several of the show's most popular songs for a Season 2 episode and even released a special "The Rocky Horror Glee Show" EP.

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

bullets: Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

slides.title: Previous Attempts at Adaptation
bullets: This isn't the first attempt at adapting 'The Rocky Horror Picture Show'.
In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

slides.speaker_notes: The remake is a new attempt at adapting the classic film, following previous attempts that did not come to fruition.

slides.title: Upcoming Live Musical Productions
bullets: Fox also has a live musical production of 'Grease', starring Julianne Hough and Vanessa Hudgens, scheduled to air on January 31, 2016.
NBC recently announced plans to air a live version of 'The Wiz' later this year.
These productions follow in the footsteps of 'The Sound of Music' and 'Peter Pan', which have also been adapted into live musical productions.
slides.speaker_notes: These upcoming productions demonstrate the ongoing interest in live musical adaptations of classic films and stage shows.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.
evidence.text:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

evidence.chunk_content:
This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

Fox's "Glee" covered several of the show's most popular songs for a Season 2 episode and even released a special "The Rocky Horror Glee Show" EP.

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.
evidence.text:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

evidence.chunk_content:
This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

Fox's "Glee" covered several of the show's most popular songs for a Season 2 episode and even released a special "The Rocky Horror Glee Show" EP.

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

evidence.chunk_content:
This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

Fox's "Glee" covered several of the show's most popular songs for a Season 2 episode and even released a special "The Rocky Horror Glee Show" EP.

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

evidence.chunk_content:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.
evidence.text:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

evidence.chunk_content:
This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

Fox's "Glee" covered several of the show's most popular songs for a Season 2 episode and even released a special "The Rocky Horror Glee Show" EP.

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.
evidence.text:
(The Hollywood Reporter)"The Rocky Horror Picture Show" is the latest musical getting the small-screen treatment.

Fox is developing a two-hour remake of the 1975 cult classic to be directed, executive-produced and choreographed by Kenneth Ortega ("High School Musical").

The project, tentatively titled "The Rocky Horror Picture Show Event," is casting-contingent.

The special will be filmed in advance and not air live, but few details beyond that are known.

evidence.chunk_content:
In addition to Ortega, Gail Berman and Lou Adler, who produced the original film, are also attached as executive producers.

The special will be produced by Fox 21 Television Studios, and Berman's The Jackal Group.

The special is timed to celebrate the 40th anniversary of the film, which has grossed more than $112 million and still plays in theaters across the country.

TV premiere dates: The complete guide .

evidence.chunk_content:
This isn't the first stab at adapting "The Rocky Horror Picture Show." In 2002, Fox unveiled plans for an adaptation timed to the 30th anniversary that never came to fruition.

The faces of pilot season 2015 .

Fox's "Glee" covered several of the show's most popular songs for a Season 2 episode and even released a special "The Rocky Horror Glee Show" EP.

There is no plan yet for when the adaptation will air.

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

Mr Anderson said that his claim was no about getting more money, but about protecting his lucrative public sector pension pot.

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

evidence.chunk_content:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

evidence.chunk_content:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

Mr Anderson said that his claim was no about getting more money, but about protecting his lucrative public sector pension pot.

evidence.chunk_content:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

evidence.chunk_content:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

Mr Anderson said that his claim was no about getting more money, but about protecting his lucrative public sector pension pot.

evidence.chunk_content:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

evidence.chunk_content:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.
evidence.text:
Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, claimed £4,500 per year from Chesterfield High School, Merseyside, despite doing nothing for pupils .

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.
evidence.text:

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.

evidence.chunk_content:
He eventually rose through the ranks to become full-time leader of the council in 2010, effectively stopping his role as a mentor, but he continued taking payments from his former employer.

When the school became an academy in 2011, and therefore had greater freedom over its finances, it ceased paying Mr Anderson, leading to his discrimination claim.

Mr Anderson said that his claim was no about getting more money, but about protecting his lucrative public sector pension pot.

A Labour mayor who campaigned against austerity while being paid an £80,000 salary took  £4,500 per year from a school where he previously worked, despite doing nothing for pupils.

Joe Anderson, 56, the Mayor of Liverpool, attempted to justify the payments by saying he provided the school with 'kudos' for being linked to him.

evidence.chunk_content:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.
evidence.text:
And when Chesterfield High School in Crosby, Merseyside, stopped the payments in 2011, he attempted to sue them, claiming discrimination because of his 'philosophical belief' in public service.

The details of the case, published in The Times, came after Mr Anderson rejected an employment tribunal ruling against him and took his case to appeal, which was also rejected.

evidence.chunk_content:
In the most recent case, Judge Daniel Serota ruled that outsiders would consider the payments a 'misapplication of public monies ' and that the school was right to stop them.

He added that he had repeatedly asked Mr Anderson's lawyers to state what benefits the school got in return for their cash.

He said: 'The only answer that I received was that it gave 'kudos' to the school.' Mr Anderson had been a senior learning mentor at the school from 2001, when he was already a Liverpool councillor.
evidence.text:
